title: AutoAnchor: Stable Diffusion Unlearning Using Cross-Attention as a Manifold Surrogate

paper.title: AutoAnchor: Stable Diffusion Unlearning Using Cross-Attention as a Manifold Surrogate
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion unlearning is essential for mitigating the generation of harmful or copyrighted content in text-to-image models. Current diffusion unlearning techniques determine the model update direction by either using alternatives of the target concept as an anchor or using empty prompts. The anchor-based method relies on manually and semantically-chosen anchors that risk biased unlearning, while the anchor-free method inherently suffers from unrobust unlearning due to unconstrained latent updates. In this work, we theoretically formalize such unstable diffusion unlearning issues under the manifold hypothesis and prove that lacking a manifold-proximal anchor inevitably induces significant normal-space drift that degrades unlearning performance. To achieve stable unlearning, we propose AutoAnchor, a two-stage framework that automatically synthesizes manifold-proximal anchors. However, direct geometric manifold optimization is computationally intractable. To address this challenge, AutoAnchor introduces a novel cross-attention consistency loss which serves as a highly efficient surrogate of manifold proximity. Experimental results demonstrate that AutoAnchor effectively achieves robust and unbiased unlearning across various state-of-the-art baselines, significantly improving targeted concept removal (by up to 31.04% in CLIP score) and non-target utility (by up to 4.18% in CLIP score). Moreover, AutoAnchor can also be easily integrated into existing diffusion unlearning methods to enhance their unlearning performance (by 6.30% for concept removal and 6.65% for utility on average).

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text-to-Image diffusion models have achieved remarkable success in generating high-fidelity images conditioned on input text prompts. However, their reliance on massive and uncurated web data introduces significant risks, e.g. , generating harmful content or copyright infringement. To mitigate these risks, diffusion unlearning has emerged as a crucial technique. The goal of diffusion unlearning is to erase a diffusion model’s ability to generate specific target concepts, which is usually realized by tuning the model parameters towards certain update directions. Achieving effective erasure while preserving model utility is hard for diffusion unlearning. This is because the modern diffusion models operate in a high-dimensional latent space, but the valid and realistic images reside on a low-dimensional data manifold within that. Without a carefully designed update direction, diffusion unlearning can easily push the model off the data manifold when erasing target concepts, thereby degrading the erasure effectiveness and damaging the model’s utility. Regarding how to determine the update directions, current diffusion unlearning methods are categorized into anchor-free unlearning and anchor-based unlearning. Anchor-free methods ( e.g., [ 13 , 15 , 29 ] ) utilize target-irrelevant directions for unlearning, simply pushing the generation away from the target concepts. For example, they tune the models toward valid but unconditional images when given prompts containing target concepts. While computationally straightforward, such update directions inherently cause off-manifold drift and lead to unrobust unlearning , manifesting as catastrophic forgetting [ 16 ] , degraded image quality [ 10 , 27 ] , and weakened text-image alignment [ 22 , 15 ] on non-target concepts. Moreover, such methods risk fragile forgetting that can be easily bypassed by adversarial prompts [ 6 , 50 , 54 ] or simple fine-tuning [ 34 ] . Existing Anchor-based methods ( e.g., [ 23 , 31 , 50 ] ) redirect the model from the target concept toward a specific alternative concept (the anchor), trying to stay on the manifold during unlearning. However, the anchors that they heavily rely on are all manually chosen based on semantic similarity, which is insufficient for ensuring manifold proximity and risks biased unlearning . With biased anchors, the unlearning can still suffer from the unrobust unlearning issues above and may further cause imprecise forgetting [ 49 ] . Both approaches suffer from a shared limitation: the inability to identify a manifold-proximal anchor for robust and unbiased unlearning. To fill this gap, we analyze the unlearning process under the manifold hypothesis. Geometrically, valid images lie on a low-dimensional data manifold within the vast diffusion latent space, as illustrated in Figure 1 . A robust and effective unlearning update should smoothly traverse along this manifold to alter target concepts, rather than pushing the representation away from it. Therefore, we decompose the unlearning update directions into their tangential (along the manifold) and normal (orthogonal to the manifold) components. Our analysis demonstrates that lacking a manifold-proximal anchor ( e.g. , anchor-free methods and unlearning via bias anchors) fundamentally leads to normal-space drift, forcing the generation trajectory off the manifold. Moreover, we prove that manifold-proximal anchors effectively align unlearning directions closely with the local tangent space of the data manifold, promoting robust and unbiased unlearning. Figure 1 : Illustration of the data manifold and unlearning update directions. Without a manifold-proximal anchor ( e.g. , our AutoAnchor), the update direction has a large normal component that pushes the model off the manifold, leading to unrobust or biased unlearning. However, constructing such a manifold-proximal anchor presents non-trivial challenges. Direct optimization on the data manifold is computationally intractable [ 9 , 20 , 35 ] , as the manifold is only implicitly defined by the complex distribution of the diffusion model’s latent space. Furthermore, there exists a fundamental domain gap: while the unlearning update operates in the diffusion latent space, the anchor is optimized within the vast prompt embedding space. To bridge this gap, our key insight is that in diffusion architectures, a frozen model’s cross-attention maps explicitly dictate the layout of certain concepts when generating images, which implicitly reflect the data manifold learned by the model. By leveraging additional semantic constraints, these attention maps serve as a powerful and efficient proxy for tangential manifold proximity (as we prove in Appendix A.7 ), enabling us to optimize an anchor that aligns its attention patterns with those of the target concept. To this end, we propose AutoAnchor, a lightweight two-stage process that automatically synthesizes manifold-proximal anchors for diffusion unlearning. It first filters and aggregates valid candidate concepts automatically, and then optimizes the anchors to be manifold-proximal to the target concept. We further propose a cross-attention consistency loss, a novel manifold optimization surrogate specific to anchor construction. AutoAnchor empirically mitigates off-manifold drift and thus effectively achieves robust and unbiased diffusion unlearning. Moreover, it can be integrated into existing diffusion unlearning methods to further improve their unlearning performance. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • Theoretical Formalization of Diffusion Unlearning Issues: We analyze diffusion unlearning via the manifold hypothesis and theoretically prove that lacking a manifold-proximal anchor inevitably causes normal-space drift, providing a mathematical explanation for why existing anchor-free and manual anchor-based methods fundamentally suffer from unstable diffusion unlearning. • Novel Manifold-Proximal Surrogate and Unlearning Framework: To overcome the computational intractability and domain gap of direct manifold optimization, we introduce a cross-attention consistency loss. Using this surrogate loss, our proposed AutoAnchor efficiently and automatically constructs manifold-proximal anchors for achieving unbiased and robust diffusion unlearning. Furthermore, we theoretically explain how AutoAnchor approximates manifold proximity. • Empirical Evaluation: Extensive experiments show that AutoAnchor improves the diffusion unlearning performance of the state-of-the-art baselines in both concept removal (improving 6.30% in CLIP score on average) and model utility (improving 6.65% in CLIP score on average). Moreover, ablation studies show the effects of cross-attention loss and its robustness on hyperparameters.

sections.heading: 2 Related Works
sections.text: Based on how to determine the update direction, existing diffusion unlearning methods are categorized into anchor-free and anchor-based approaches. Anchor-free approaches determine their update directions using coarse signals like empty prompts, generic concepts, or unconditional scores. For example, ESD [ 13 ] utilizes the difference of predictions between the target concept and empty prompt as the update direction. Such imprecise directions cause a series of robustness issues in diffusion unlearning (unrobust against adversarial prompts, etc ). Although existing works have made efforts to address them, they target individual issues in isolation. Specifically, [ 54 ] only focuses on robustness against adversarial prompts; [ 22 , 16 , 41 , 1 , 10 ] only aim to strengthen model utility; [ 30 ] is solely concerned with utility loss after multiple unlearning; and [ 34 , 14 , 51 ] only pursue effective concept removal. No single existing work solves these issues simultaneously, due to ignoring the root problem of imprecise update directions. Our method fundamentally fills this gap by generating a stable anchor for precise unlearning direction, thereby enabling robust diffusion unlearning. Anchor-based approaches pre-define specific anchor concepts for the target concepts, aiming to provide more precise unlearning directions than anchor-free methods. For example, ConAbl [ 23 ] first uses the generation direction differences between the target and anchor concepts as the update direction, thus realizing better utility preservation than ESD. Recent anchor-based methods further explore more sophisticated problems like reliable erasure [ 19 , 50 , 29 , 49 ] , multiple unlearning [ 47 , 15 ] , training-free unlearning [ 4 ] , concept erosion [ 31 , 36 , 46 , 27 ] , and attention-based unlearning [ 52 , 53 ] . However, existing anchor-based methods heavily rely on the assumption that their manually chosen anchors are precise. This assumption is not practical when semantically close anchors are not manifold-proximal to the target concepts, leading to biased unlearning as we show in Appendix § B.2 . While some works [ 49 , 31 , 28 , 21 ] attempt to generate anchors automatically, they still rely on semantic closeness and thus fail to provide fundamentally unbiased anchors. Our method leverages cross-attention maps as a practical manifold surrogate that manages to construct manifold-proximal anchors, thereby achieving unbiased unlearning. Moreover, our method can be easily integrated into existing diffusion unlearning methods to further improve their unlearning performance.

sections.heading: 3 Preliminaries
sections.text: Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs). Modern text-to-image models ( e.g. , Stable Diffusion [ 39 ] ) operate in a compressed latent space. Given an input text prompt, the model first maps it into the corresponding embedding 𝐞 ∈ ℰ \mathbf{e}\in\mathcal{E} . Next, the model predicts the latent noise ϵ ∈ ℝ d \epsilon\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , which is then used to generate an image latent 𝐳 ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} as the output. sections.heading: 4 Theoretical Analysis of Unstable Diffusion Unlearning
sections.text: In § 4.1 , we first introduce the manifold notations and statistical assumptions. Next we theoretically analyze why existing diffusion unlearning methods are unstable in § 4.2 . In § 4.3 , we further prove that unlearning updates determined by manifold-proximal anchors successfully mitigate this instability. Complete proofs, detailed assumption justifications, and extra stability analyses are in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 5 Design of AutoAnchor
sections.text: To fundamentally avoid the instability and bias problems in diffusion unlearning, the anchor generated by AutoAnchor must satisfy three key requirements. (R1) Non-Synonymous: It must not be a direct synonym of the target concept. For example, using “naked” as an anchor fails to unlearn the "nude" concept, because the two distributions largely overlap, leaving the target insufficiently suppressed. (R2) Semantic Alternative: It should be a valid semantic alternative related to the target concept. For example, using an irrelevant concept “Mickey Mouse” as an anchor to unlearn the “nude” concept offers no meaningful guidance and effectively behaves as unconditional noise. (R3) Manifold-Proximal: It should be manifold-proximal to the target concept to guide a stable unlearning direction, as demonstrated by our theoretical analysis in § 4 . In addition to the three requirements of the anchor above, the generation process itself must be automatic (to avoid manually introducing extra subjective bias and ensure scalability of unlearning) and efficient (acting as a lightweight preprocessing step). To meet these criteria, we propose a two-stage framework, illustrated in Figure 2 . The first stage initializes the anchor by clustering and aggregating a diverse set of candidate concepts (§ 5.1 ), explicitly enforcing R1 and R2 . The second stage optimizes the initial anchor to approach manifold proximity using a cross-attention surrogate (§ 5.2 ), thereby satisfying R3 . Finally, we apply AutoAnchor to unlearn the target concept from the model, achieving robust and unbiased unlearning. Figure 2 : Illustration of AutoAnchor. Given a target concept c u c_{u} to unlearn, AutoAnchor first generates, filters, and aggregates the candidate concepts. Then AutoAnchor optimizes the cross-attention consistency loss ℒ CA \mathcal{L}_{\rm CA} for R3 and a regularization term ℒ reg \mathcal{L}_{\rm reg} to maintain R1 and R2 . Finally, with AutoAnchor, we tune the model parameters to achieve robust and unbiased diffusion unlearning.

sections.text: Baselines & Diffusion Models. We compare AutoAnchor against seven state-of-the-art diffusion unlearning baselines: four anchor-free methods (ESD [ 13 ] , TuneSD-AF (anchor-free) [ 41 ] , ResAlign [ 29 ] , and CCRT [ 15 ] ) and three anchor-based methods (ConAbl [ 23 ] , FMN [ 52 ] and TuneSD-AB (anchor-based) [ 41 ] ). These baselines were primarily built on SD v1.4 and focused on erasing specific concept categories, including copyrighted characters (e.g., Mickey Mouse), artistic styles (e.g., Van Gogh), and unsafe content (e.g., nudity). We adopt the same settings to ensure a fair comparison. Evaluation Metrics. Following standard evaluation protocols, we assess model performance using CLIP scores and the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID). A higher CLIP score indicates better text-image semantic alignment, while a lower FID indicates superior image quality. We evaluate the models based on two primary criteria: (1) Removal : The model should fail to generate the erased concept, resulting in a low CLIP score on target concept prompts. (2) Utility Preservation : The model must retain its general generative capabilities on non-target concepts, which requires maintaining high text-image alignment (a high CLIP score) alongside high image quality (a low FID score). In the following sections, we first present the main experiment results in § 6.1 , demonstrating AutoAnchor’s superior unlearning performance against state-of-the-art baselines. In § 6.2 , we conduct an ablation study to validate the necessity of our two-stage design. Next, in § 6.3 , we quantitatively confirm that AutoAnchor is highly efficient and practical for real-world deployment. Our method and baselines augmented with AutoAnchor achieve robust target erasure while preserving non-target image quality and text alignment. Table 1 quantitatively shows the evaluation result on the three distinct unlearning targets. We denote the CLIP scores for target concepts and non-target concepts as CLIP(U) and CLIP(R), respectively. Enhanced Concept Removal. First, AutoAnchor consistently achieves the lowest or second lowest CLIP(U) score among all diffusion unlearning methods across all three target concepts (improving “Mickey Mouse” by 31.04% compared to the top baseline), demonstrating superior unlearning efficacy. Second, when augmented with AutoAnchor, all baselines show a consistent improvement in CLIP(U) scores (6.30% for Mickey Mouse, 6.28% for Van Gogh, and 3.59% for the nude concept on average), indicating that AutoAnchor effectively enhances the unlearning performance of existing methods. Improved Model Utility. First, AutoAnchor always achieves the best or second best CLIP(R) score and FID score comparing with the baselines, which shows that AutoAnchor successfully preserve models’ text-image alignment and image utility on non-target concepts (improving FID score on “Van Gogh style” by 4.18% compared to the top baseline). Besides, Figure 3 visually validate the superior performance of AutoAnchor. Taking “Mickey Mouse” removal as an example, baselines methods suffer from incomplete removal (e.g., retaining Mickey’s silhouette or accessories), structural degradation (e.g., no piano), or degraded image quality. In contrast AutoAnchor precisely erases the concept without sacrificing non-target utility. Moreover, after integrated with AutoAnchor, all baselines consistently generate clean and semantically relevant images with no trace of the copyrighted character, demonstrating robust and unbiased removal.

The results demonstrate that relying solely on semantically aggregated anchors (the ∗ * variant) frequently induces severe unlearning bias, leading to stagnant or degraded removal efficacy. This is particularly evident in anchor-based methods (ConAbl, FMN, and tuneSD-AB), where the unoptimized semantic anchor actively harms concept removal, causing CLIP(U) to increase by 1.43%, 9.44%, and 6.63%, respectively. These failures empirically validate our argument in § 1 that semantically selected anchors can not guarantee manifold proximity. Cross-Attention as a Manifold Surrogate. By introducing the second stage of optimization (the + + variant), AutoAnchor significantly improves the concept removal from a marginal 0.55% degradation to a robust 6.28% reduction, while simultaneously boosting average utility preservation (CLIP(R) score) from 3.31% to 5.31%. This substantial contrast provides compelling evidence that our proposed cross-attention consistency loss effectively functions as a tractable surrogate for manifold proximity. By minimizing this loss, we successfully guides the anchor into a latent region that is manifold-proximal to the target concept, thereby guaranteeing unbiased and robust unlearning.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we theoretically established that unconstrained normal-space drift causes unrobust diffusion unlearning in anchor-free methods and biased unlearning in anchor-based methods with manually chosen anchors. The core solution is to construct a manifold-proximal anchor that provides a stable unlearning direction. To this end, we propose AutoAnchor, an automated diffusion unlearning framework that uses our cross-attention consistency surrogate loss to efficiently synthesize manifold-proximal anchors. Extensive empirical evaluations confirm that AutoAnchor achieves robust and unbiased diffusion unlearning efficiently. Moreover, AutoAnchor can also be integrated into existing diffusion unlearning methods to further improve their performance.

sections.heading: Appendix A Appendix of Theoretical Analysis
sections.text: This appendix provides the formal justifications for our statistical assumptions, the complete absolute magnitude bounds for both anchor-free and ζ \zeta -proximal unlearning updates, and the rigorous random-walk proofs establishing the trajectory stability of the unlearning process. All detailed proofs are consolidated in Appendix A.6 .

sections.heading: A.1 Details of Problem Setup
sections.text: To provides more details of assumptions and their formal justifications, we extend the definition, which is consistent with § 3 and § 4 . Manifold Notations : Let ( ℝ d , ∥ ⋅ ∥ ) (\mathbb{R}^{d},\|\cdot\|) denote the d d -dimensional Euclidean space equipped with the standard Euclidean norm. We consider data sampled from an unknown distribution μ data \mu_{\text{data}} supported on a smooth, compact manifold ℳ ⊂ ℝ d \mathcal{M}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} . For a target concept c u c_{u} , we denote by ℳ u ⊂ ℳ \mathcal{M}_{u}\subset\mathcal{M} the concept-specific submanifold consisting of all data points associated with target concept c u c_{u} . The intrinsic dimension of ℳ u \mathcal{M}_{u} is denoted by d u ∗ d_{u}^{*} . In practice, d u ∗ ≪ d d_{u}^{*}\ll d due to the manifold hypothesis. Geometric Decomposition : To analyze the stability of unlearning updates, we decompose the gradient directions relative to the target concept manifold ℳ u \mathcal{M}_{u} . For any point 𝐳 u ∈ ℳ \mathbf{z}_{u}\in\mathcal{M} , T u ​ ℳ T_{u}\mathcal{M} denotes the d u ∗ d_{u}^{*} -dimensional tangent space (directions along the manifold), while N u ​ ℳ N_{u}\mathcal{M} denotes the ( d − d u ∗ ) (d-d_{u}^{*}) -dimensional normal space (the orthogonal complement). For any update vector v ∈ ℝ d v\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , we define its orthogonal projections: v T \displaystyle v_{T} = Π T ( v ) = Proj T u ​ ℳ ( v ) ∈ T u ℳ (tangential component) \displaystyle=\Pi_{T}(v)=\text{Proj}_{T_{u}\mathcal{M}}(v)\in T_{u}\mathcal{M}\quad\text{(tangential component)} (7) v N \displaystyle v_{N} = Π N ( v ) = Proj N u ​ ℳ ( v ) ∈ N u ℳ (normal component) \displaystyle=\Pi_{N}(v)=\text{Proj}_{N_{u}\mathcal{M}}(v)\in N_{u}\mathcal{M}\quad\text{(normal component)} (8) The Π \Pi is denoted as the projection operator. The geometric intuition is fundamental: tangential updates ( v N ≈ 0 v_{N}\approx 0 ) safely traverse the manifold to alter concept semantics while preserving valid data properties. Normal updates ( v T ≈ 0 v_{T}\approx 0 ) push the generated trajectory off the manifold, fundamentally degrading sample quality and leading to unlearning instability. Here we formally provide the definition of ζ \zeta -proximal anchor, which is first used in § 4.3 . Definition 1 ( ζ \zeta -Proximal Anchor) . A concept representation a ∗ ∈ 𝒞 a^{*}\in\mathcal{C} is a ζ \zeta -proximal anchor for concept c c if for all latent state z t z_{t} in the support of p t ( ⋅ | c ) p_{t}(\cdot|c) (i.e., z t ∈ ℳ u z_{t}\in\mathcal{M}_{u} ): 𝔼 t ∼ 𝒰 [ 0 , T ] , 𝐳 t ∼ p t ( ⋅ ∣ c ) [ ‖ Π N ​ ( ϵ θ ∗ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , 𝐞 u ) − ϵ θ ∗ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , 𝐞 a ∗ ) ) ‖ 2 ‖ ϵ θ ∗ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , 𝐞 u ) − ϵ θ ∗ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , 𝐞 a ∗ ) ‖ 2 + ε ] ≤ ζ 2 , \mathbb{E}_{t\sim\mathcal{U}[0,T],\mathbf{z}_{t}\sim p_{t}(\cdot\mid c)}\left[\frac{\left\|\Pi_{N}\left(\epsilon_{\theta^{*}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{e}_{u})-\epsilon_{\theta^{*}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{e}_{a^{*}})\right)\right\|^{2}}{\left\|\epsilon_{\theta^{*}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{e}_{u})-\epsilon_{\theta^{*}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{e}_{a^{*}})\right\|^{2}+\varepsilon}\right]\leq\zeta^{2}, (9) where ε > 0 \varepsilon>0 is a small numerical stabilizer. The expectation is taken over both time steps t t and latent states 𝐳 t \mathbf{z}_{t} conditioned on the target concept. The 𝐞 a ∗ \mathbf{e}_{a^{*}} is the embedding of the anchor concept a ∗ a^{*} , and ζ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ) \zeta\in[0,1) bounds the degree of normal misalignment. This means that for all valid latent states related to the target concept, the noise prediction difference between the target and the anchor is predominantly aligned with the tangent space, with at most ζ \zeta fraction of its energy in the normal direction. Therefore, an important property of this definition is that ζ \zeta also quantifies how proximal the anchor is to the target concept. For a ζ \zeta -proximal anchor, the normalized unlearning update v PA = Δ AB / ‖ Δ AB ‖ v_{\text{PA}}=\Delta^{\text{AB}}/\|\Delta^{\text{AB}}\| is predominantly aligned with the tangent space, satisfying: 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ Π N ​ ( v PA ) ‖ 2 ] ≤ ζ 2 + d u ∗ d . \mathbb{E}\left[\|\Pi_{N}(v_{\text{PA}})\|^{2}\right]\leq\zeta^{2}+\frac{d_{u}^{*}}{d}. sections.heading: A.2 Extended Statistical Assumptions and Justifications
sections.text: Our theoretical framework relies on the following assumptions, which formalize the geometric and statistical properties of diffusion models operating in high-dimensional latent spaces. Assumption ( 1 with Justification) . The ambient dimension d d is much larger than the intrinsic dimension d u ∗ d_{u}^{*} of the concept manifold. Formally, d u ∗ d → 0 \frac{d_{u}^{*}}{d}\to 0 as d → ∞ d\to\infty . Justification: Real-world data such as images typically lie near low-dimensional manifolds with intrinsic dimensions on the order of 10 2 10^{2} to 10 3 10^{3} , whereas the ambient dimension is vastly larger ( d ≈ 16,384 d\approx 16,384 for Stable Diffusion v1.4 latent spaces, or > 200,000 >200,000 for pixel space). This dimensional disparity is well-established in manifold learning theory and empirical studies [ 38 , 2 , 12 ] . Assumption ( 2 with Justification) . The neural network approximation error decomposes as: ϵ θ ​ ( z t , c , t ) = ∇ z t ​ log ​ p t ​ ( z t | c ) + ε u ​ ( z t , t ) , \epsilon_{\theta}(z_{t},c,t)=\nabla_{z_{t}}\log p_{t}(z_{t}|c)+\varepsilon_{u}(z_{t},t), (11) where ε u ​ ( z t , t ) ∈ ℝ d \varepsilon_{u}(z_{t},t)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is a zero-mean random vector representing the approximation error, with covariance structure: Cov ​ ( ε u ​ ( z t , t ) ) = σ est 2 ​ [ α u ​ Π T u + ( 1 − α u ) ​ I d ] . \text{Cov}(\varepsilon_{u}(z_{t},t))=\sigma_{\text{est}}^{2}\left[\alpha_{u}\Pi_{T_{u}}+(1-\alpha_{u})I_{d}\right]. (12) Here: • σ est 2 > 0 \sigma_{\text{est}}^{2}>0 is the estimation variance, quantifying the overall magnitude of approximation error. • α u ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \alpha_{u}\in[0,1] measures the alignment of errors with the tangent space. When α u = 1 \alpha_{u}=1 , errors are confined to the tangent space; when α u = 0 \alpha_{u}=0 , errors are isotropic. • Π T u \Pi_{T_{u}} is the projection operator onto the tangent space T u ​ ℳ T_{u}\mathcal{M} . • I d I_{d} is the d × d d\times d identity matrix. Justification: Theoretical analyses of diffusion models demonstrate that score functions inherently decompose into components governing tangent-space distribution and normal-space projection [ 37 , 43 ] . Consequently, the approximation error is highly anisotropic; errors in recovering the manifold geometry differ fundamentally in magnitude from errors in recovering the tangent distribution [ 8 , 33 ] . Assumption ( 3 with Justification) . For anchor-free unlearning, the normalized update vector v AF = Δ AF / ‖ Δ AF ‖ v_{\text{AF}}=\Delta^{\text{AF}}/\|\Delta^{\text{AF}}\| is approximately isotropic. Specifically, for any fixed m m -dimensional subspace V ⊂ ℝ d V\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} and margin δ > 0 \delta>0 : ℙ ⁡ ( ‖ Π V ​ ( v AF ) ‖ 2 ≥ ( 1 + δ ) ​ m d ) ≤ exp ⁡ ( − κ 0 ​ m ​ δ 2 ) , \mathbb{P}\left(\|\Pi_{V}(v_{\text{AF}})\|^{2}\geq(1+\delta)\frac{m}{d}\right)\leq\exp\left(-\kappa_{0}m\delta^{2}\right), (13) where κ 0 > 0 \kappa_{0}>0 is a universal constant. Justification: While neural networks possess strong inductive biases, in highly overparameterized regimes, the unconstrained difference between complex, misaligned functions (such as the conditional target score and the unconditional score) exhibits quasi-random geometric behavior relative to specific low-dimensional submanifolds. As established in high-dimensional probability [ 7 , 48 ] , this interference bleeds nearly uniformly into all orthogonal subspaces. This structurally explains the catastrophic interference observed in anchor-free methods [ 13 ] . Assumption 4 (Manifold Regularity) . The target concept manifold ℳ u \mathcal{M}_{u} has reach τ > 0 \tau>0 and bounded sectional curvature κ max < ∞ \kappa_{\max}<\infty . Justification: The assumption of positive reach and bounded curvature is a standard regularity condition in geometric measure theory, ensuring the manifold is sufficiently smooth and devoid of self-intersecting singularities [ 32 , 11 ] . A strictly positive reach τ \tau guarantees the existence of a well-defined tubular neighborhood around ℳ u \mathcal{M}_{u} wherein the metric projection onto the manifold remains unique.

sections.heading: B.2 Case Study: Bias Unlearning
sections.text: In this section, we present a case study to show that anchor-based methods using manually chosen anchors risk bias unlearning. We take target concept “grumpy” as an example, which is used in ConAbl, the first anchor-based diffusion unlearning. We collect these manually chosen anchors (including “-”, “angry”, “tired”, “cold”, “quiet”, and “happy”) from existing diffusion unlearning works [ 23 ] and LLMs. Obviously, these anchors are semantically close to the target “grumpy” and are intuitive to humans. The “-” here means empty prompt, which is collected from the example using “cat” as the anchor for “grumpy cat” in [ 23 ] . sections.heading: B.4 Extra Ablation Study on Hyperparameters
sections.text: In the Stage I of AutoAnchor, as introduced in § 5.1 , we finally select the top K K most frequently predicted tokens as the candidate set C 0 C_{0} for initializing the anchor embedding 𝐞 a 0 \mathbf{e}_{a}^{0} . Therefore, the number of K K seems to be naturally essential for the performance of AutoAnchor. To this end, we further conduct this ablation study to show the impact of K K on the performance of AutoAnchor. As shown in Table 7 , we test the unlearning performance when K = 5 , 10 , 20 , 30 K=5,10,20,30 . For K K with small value (like 5, 10), the unlearning performance of AutoAnchoris relatively weakened: the original AutoAnchor method can not achieve the best or second best for both removal and utility; there is also no obvious improvement for existing methods augmented with AutoAnchor . However, when K K is a little bit larger (20 and 30), AutoAnchor’s unlearning performance is significantly strengthen: the original AutoAnchor method consistently achieves the best or second best for both removal and utility; existing methods augmented with AutoAnchor also consistently improve the concept removal (4.35% and 5,45% improvement in CLIP(U) scores) and model utility performance (4.85% and 3.48% improvement in CLIP(R) scores; 3.16% and 1.26% improvement in FID scores). This indicates that too few candidates can not effectively initialize the anchor embedding 𝐞 a 0 \mathbf{e}_{a}^{0} to be a good starting point for optimization. This is reasonable, for example, when K = 5 K=5 , there will be difficult to cluster among them. There will also be no enough candidates remaining in C 1 C_{1} for initializing the anchor embedding 𝐞 a 0 \mathbf{e}_{a}^{0} after filtering while satisfying R1 and R2 . It is also noted that too many candidates (like K = 30 K=30 ) just leads to marginal improvement compared to K = 20 K=20 . Too many candidates no longer provide more useful information for initializing the anchor embedding 𝐞 a 0 \mathbf{e}_{a}^{0} and thus does not lead to significant improvement. Therefore, AutoAnchor is relatively robust to the choice of K K as long as it is not too small, which further validates the robustness of AutoAnchor in enhancing the performance of existing algorithms regardless of the choice of hyperparameters. sections.text: In this section, we present a detailed case study on unlearning the “Porsche” concept as an example to illustrate the workflow and design of AutoAnchor . As we introduced in § 5 , AutoAnchor operates in two stages: it first initializes the anchor embedding 𝐞 a 0 \mathbf{e}_{a}^{0} and then optimizes the anchor embedding 𝐞 a \mathbf{e}_{a} with the cross-attention surrogate objective. Each stage contains multiple steps, which we will explain in detail with the Porsche case below. Automatic Candidate Generation. We first use LLM (in this case, we use Gemini-3.1 pro) to generate a set of sentences 𝐲 ( i ) \mathbf{y}^{(i)} including the target concept Porsche with the prompt shown in the conversation context below, where the sentences number N N is ten. She parked her brand new Porsche right in front of the restaurant. 3. The vintage Porsche fetched a record price at the auction. 4. You can tell it’s a Porsche just by the sound of its flat-six engine. 5. They rented a sleek black Porsche for their weekend getaway to Napa. 6. Maintenance on a classic Porsche can be quite expensive. 7. He spent his entire bonus on a customized Porsche 911. 8. The racing team unveiled their latest Porsche for the upcoming Le Mans. 9. Whenever a bright yellow Porsche drives by, heads inevitably turn. 10. She carefully washed and waxed her father’s old Porsche on Sunday afternoon. For each sentence 𝐲 ( i ) \mathbf{y}^{(i)} in this set 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , we mask the concept word “Porsche” and predict the top M M tokens with the highest probabilities from the LLM. The example of the first sentence is shown in the conversation context below. Next, we aggregate the predicted tokens across all sentences and select the top K = 10 K=10 most frequently predicted tokens as the candidate set C 0 C_{0} . In this case, the C 0 C_{0} for the Porsche concept is {car, Porsche, vehicle, Ferrari, BMW, motorcycle, Audi, Mercedes, truck, convertible}. It is obvious that those concepts are typical alternatives of “Porsche” and satisfying R2 . However, it is noted that “Porsche’ itself is also involved, thereby violating R1 . Such violation will be more pronounced in the case of descriptive target concepts, e.g. , “grumpy” and “nude”. Therefore, we need to further filter the candidate set to ensure the validity of the anchor embedding. Candidate Filtering and Aggregation . We first encode the concepts in C 0 C_{0} and then apply f cluster = f_{\text{cluster}}= K-Means on those concept embeddings. The number of clusters M M is automatically determined by the silhouette score [ 40 ] , a widely accepted method in machine learning for determining cluster numbers. This algorithm measures the cohesion and separation of the clusters, which can cleanly separate synonyms from distinct semantic alternatives in the embedding space. In this case, the clustering results in two distinct clusters: Cluster 1 contains {car, vehicle, motorcycle, truck, convertible} and Cluster 2 contains {Porsche, Ferrari, BMW, Audi, Mercedes}. We then drop the cluster containing “Porsche” (Cluster 2 in this case) and form C 1 C_{1} using the concepts in the rest clusters (Cluster 1 in this case). After filtering the candidate set, we have C 1 = { c ​ a ​ r , v ​ e ​ h ​ i ​ c ​ l ​ e , m ​ o ​ t ​ o ​ r ​ c ​ y ​ c ​ l ​ e , t ​ r ​ u ​ c ​ k , c ​ o ​ n ​ v ​ e ​ r ​ t ​ i ​ b ​ l ​ e } C_{1}=\{car,vehicle,motorcycle,truck,convertible\} , which are all valid alternatives of “Porsche” and satisfying both R1 and R2 . The anchor embedding 𝐞 a 0 \mathbf{e}_{a}^{0} is then initialized by averaging the embeddings of those concepts in C 1 C_{1} . Now we have a valid anchor embedding that is semantically close to the target concept “Porsche” but does not contain the concept itself, which serves as a good starting point for the subsequent optimization stage. Calculating Regularization Parameters . Before optimization, we calculate the r − r_{-} and r + r_{+} in Equation ( 6 ) in advance, which will be used as the regularization targets in the second stage. In this case, the closest and farthest cluster of ‘‘Porsche’’ are Cluster 2 1 1 1 It is noted that the 𝐞 u \mathbf{e}_{u} ’s closest cluster centroid is always the centroid that 𝐞 u \mathbf{e}_{u} belong to. and Cluster 1, respectively. Therefore, we calculate r − r_{-} as the average cosine similarity between “Porsche” and the concepts in Cluster 2, and calculate r + r_{+} as the average cosine similarity between “Porsche” and the concepts in Cluster 1. During optimization, the anchor embedding 𝐞 a \mathbf{e}_{a} might violate R1 (approaching to the target concept itself) or R2 (being too irrelevant). By forcing the cosine distance between 𝐞 a \mathbf{e}_{a} and “Porsche” 𝐞 u \mathbf{e}_{u} to be larger than r − r_{-} , we prevent the anchor from being clustered with target concept, thereby maintaining R1 . On the other hand, the anchor embedding can not be too far from “Porsche” (violating R2 ). By setting r − r_{-} and r + r_{+} for the regularization term, we can explicitly penalize the anchor embedding if it violates R1 and R2 during optimization.

sections.heading: Appendix C Limitations
sections.text: While our framework provides formal trajectory stability guarantees for AutoAnchor, mapping abstract high-dimensional manifold geometry to concrete U-Net architectures necessitates several structural assumptions. Specifically, the analysis assumes (i) idealized regularity of the target data manifold ℳ u \mathcal{M}_{u} , (ii) strict isotropy of approximation errors, and (iii) an attention-geometry isomorphism that bounds geometric normal-space drift via cross-attention discrepancy. In particular, imposing a global Lipschitz constraint on the deep, non-linear dynamics of a U-Net is a strong abstraction; however, because direct manifold optimization is computationally intractable, this isomorphism serves as a necessary mechanism to link theoretical stability with actionable model activations. Despite these theoretical abstractions, AutoAnchor demonstrates strong robustness in practice. The massive ambient dimensionality ( d ≫ d c ∗ d\gg d_{c}^{*} ) of image latent spaces yields an exponential margin of safety, effectively mitigating local violations of manifold regularity or strict error isotropy. Furthermore, optimizing our empirical surrogate—the cross-attention consistency loss—grounds this theoretical isomorphism. By minimizing this loss, AutoAnchor tightly bounds the geometric normal drift limit ζ \zeta , driving it toward zero. This formulation successfully accommodates manifold-preserving semantic shifts while ensuring the unlearning trajectory avoids the catastrophic normal-space leakage inherent to anchor-free methods. Moreover, AutoAnchor exhibits positive social impact to protect data owner’s right to be forgotten. It also helps prevent harmful generations. However, it is noted that machine unlearning itself risks being used as a harmful mechanism by removing and hampering useful knowledge.

Affiliation: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) {swen211,jzeng110}@connect.hkust-gz.edu.cn , ningningding@hkust-gz.edu.cn Abstract Diffusion unlearning is essential for mitigating the generation of harmful or copyrighted content in text-to-image models. Current diffusion unlearning techniques determine the model update direction by either using alternatives of the target concept as an anchor or using empty prompts. The anchor-based method relies on manually and semantically-chosen anchors that risk biased unlearning, while the anchor-free method inherently suffers from unrobust unlearning due to unconstrained latent updates. In this work, we theoretically formalize such unstable diffusion unlearning issues under the manifold hypothesis and prove that lacking a manifold-proximal anchor inevitably induces significant normal-space drift that degrades unlearning performance. To achieve stable unlearning, we propose AutoAnchor, a two-stage framework that automatically synthesizes manifold-proximal anchors. However, direct geometric manifold optimization is computationally intractable. To address this challenge, AutoAnchor introduces a novel cross-attention consistency loss which serves as a highly efficient surrogate of manifold proximity. Experimental results demonstrate that AutoAnchor effectively achieves robust and unbiased unlearning across various state-of-the-art baselines, significantly improving targeted concept removal (by up to 31.04% in CLIP score) and non-target utility (by up to 4.18% in CLIP score). Moreover, AutoAnchor can also be easily integrated into existing diffusion unlearning methods to enhance their unlearning performance (by 6.30% for concept removal and 6.65% for utility on average). 1 Introduction Text-to-Image diffusion models have achieved remarkable success in generating high-fidelity images conditioned on input text prompts. However, their reliance on massive and uncurated web data introduces significant risks, e.g. , generating harmful content or copyright infringement. To mitigate these risks, diffusion unlearning has emerged as a crucial technique. The goal of diffusion unlearning is to erase a diffusion model’s ability to generate specific target concepts, which is usually realized by tuning the model parameters towards certain update directions. Achieving effective erasure while preserving model utility is hard for diffusion unlearning. This is because the modern diffusion models operate in a high-dimensional latent space, but the valid and realistic images reside on a low-dimensional data manifold within that. Without a carefully designed update direction, diffusion unlearning can easily push the model off the data manifold when erasing target concepts, thereby degrading the erasure effectiveness and damaging the model’s utility. Regarding how to determine the update directions, current diffusion unlearning methods are categorized into anchor-free unlearning and anchor-based unlearning. Anchor-free methods ( e.g., [ 13 , 15 , 29 ] ) utilize target-irrelevant directions for unlearning, simply pushing the generation away from the target concepts. For example, they tune the models toward valid but unconditional images when given prompts containing target concepts. While computationally straightforward, such update directions inherently cause off-manifold drift and lead to unrobust unlearning , manifesting as catastrophic forgetting [ 16 ] , degraded image quality [ 10 , 27 ] , and weakened text-image alignment [ 22 , 15 ] on non-target concepts. Moreover, such methods risk fragile forgetting that can be easily bypassed by adversarial prompts [ 6 , 50 , 54 ] or simple fine-tuning [ 34 ] . Existing Anchor-based methods ( e.g., [ 23 , 31 , 50 ] ) redirect the model from the target concept toward a specific alternative concept (the anchor), trying to stay on the manifold during unlearning. However, the anchors that they heavily rely on are all manually chosen based on semantic similarity, which is insufficient for ensuring manifold proximity and risks biased unlearning . With biased anchors, the unlearning can still suffer from the unrobust unlearning issues above and may further cause imprecise forgetting [ 49 ] . Both approaches suffer from a shared limitation: the inability to identify a manifold-proximal anchor for robust and unbiased unlearning. To fill this gap, we analyze the unlearning process under the manifold hypothesis. Geometrically, valid images lie on a low-dimensional data manifold within the vast diffusion latent space, as illustrated in Figure 1 . A robust and effective unlearning update should smoothly traverse along this manifold to alter target concepts, rather than pushing the representation away from it. Therefore, we decompose the unlearning update directions into their tangential (along the manifold) and normal (orthogonal to the manifold) components. Our analysis demonstrates that lacking a manifold-proximal anchor ( e.g. , anchor-free methods and unlearning via bias anchors) fundamentally leads to normal-space drift, forcing the generation trajectory off the manifold. Moreover, we prove that manifold-proximal anchors effectively align unlearning directions closely with the local tangent space of the data manifold, promoting robust and unbiased unlearning. Figure 1 : Illustration of the data manifold and unlearning update directions. Without a manifold-proximal anchor ( e.g. , our AutoAnchor), the update direction has a large normal component that pushes the model off the manifold, leading to unrobust or biased unlearning. However, constructing such a manifold-proximal anchor presents non-trivial challenges. Direct optimization on the data manifold is computationally intractable [ 9 , 20 , 35 ] , as the manifold is only implicitly defined by the complex distribution of the diffusion model’s latent space. Furthermore, there exists a fundamental domain gap: while the unlearning update operates in the diffusion latent space, the anchor is optimized within the vast prompt embedding space. To bridge this gap, our key insight is that in diffusion architectures, a frozen model’s cross-attention maps explicitly dictate the layout of certain concepts when generating images, which implicitly reflect the data manifold learned by the model. By leveraging additional semantic constraints, these attention maps serve as a powerful and efficient proxy for tangential manifold proximity (as we prove in Appendix A.7 ), enabling us to optimize an anchor that aligns its attention patterns with those of the target concept. To this end, we propose AutoAnchor, a lightweight two-stage process that automatically synthesizes manifold-proximal anchors for diffusion unlearning. It first filters and aggregates valid candidate concepts automatically, and then optimizes the anchors to be manifold-proximal to the target concept. We further propose a cross-attention consistency loss, a novel manifold optimization surrogate specific to anchor construction. AutoAnchor empirically mitigates off-manifold drift and thus effectively achieves robust and unbiased diffusion unlearning. Moreover, it can be integrated into existing diffusion unlearning methods to further improve their unlearning performance. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • Theoretical Formalization of Diffusion Unlearning Issues: We analyze diffusion unlearning via the manifold hypothesis and theoretically prove that lacking a manifold-proximal anchor inevitably causes normal-space drift, providing a mathematical explanation for why existing anchor-free and manual anchor-based methods fundamentally suffer from unstable diffusion unlearning. • Novel Manifold-Proximal Surrogate and Unlearning Framework: To overcome the computational intractability and domain gap of direct manifold optimization, we introduce a cross-attention consistency loss. Using this surrogate loss, our proposed AutoAnchor efficiently and automatically constructs manifold-proximal anchors for achieving unbiased and robust diffusion unlearning. Furthermore, we theoretically explain how AutoAnchor approximates manifold proximity. • Empirical Evaluation: Extensive experiments show that AutoAnchor improves the diffusion unlearning performance of the state-of-the-art baselines in both concept removal (improving 6.30% in CLIP score on average) and model utility (improving 6.65% in CLIP score on average). Moreover, ablation studies show the effects of cross-attention loss and its robustness on hyperparameters. 2 Related Works Based on how to determine the update direction, existing diffusion unlearning methods are categorized into anchor-free and anchor-based approaches. Anchor-free approaches determine their update directions using coarse signals like empty prompts, generic concepts, or unconditional scores. For example, ESD [ 13 ] utilizes the difference of predictions between the target concept and empty prompt as the update direction. Such imprecise directions cause a series of robustness issues in diffusion unlearning (unrobust against adversarial prompts, etc ). Although existing works have made efforts to address them, they target individual issues in isolation. Specifically, [ 54 ] only focuses on robustness against adversarial prompts; [ 22 , 16 , 41 , 1 , 10 ] only aim to strengthen model utility; [ 30 ] is solely concerned with utility loss after multiple unlearning; and [ 34 , 14 , 51 ] only pursue effective concept removal. No single existing work solves these issues simultaneously, due to ignoring the root problem of imprecise update directions. Our method fundamentally fills this gap by generating a stable anchor for precise unlearning direction, thereby enabling robust diffusion unlearning. Anchor-based approaches pre-define specific anchor concepts for the target concepts, aiming to provide more precise unlearning directions than anchor-free methods. For example, ConAbl [ 23 ] first uses the generation direction differences between the target and anchor concepts as the update direction, thus realizing better utility preservation than ESD. Recent anchor-based methods further explore more sophisticated problems like reliable erasure [ 19 , 50 , 29 , 49 ] , multiple unlearning [ 47 , 15 ] , training-free unlearning [ 4 ] , concept erosion [ 31 , 36 , 46 , 27 ] , and attention-based unlearning [ 52 , 53 ] . However, existing anchor-based methods heavily rely on the assumption that their manually chosen anchors are precise. This assumption is not practical when semantically close anchors are not manifold-proximal to the target concepts, leading to biased unlearning as we show in Appendix § B.2 . While some works [ 49 , 31 , 28 , 21 ] attempt to generate anchors automatically, they still rely on semantic closeness and thus fail to provide fundamentally unbiased anchors. Our method leverages cross-attention maps as a practical manifold surrogate that manages to construct manifold-proximal anchors, thereby achieving unbiased unlearning. Moreover, our method can be easily integrated into existing diffusion unlearning methods to further improve their unlearning performance. 3 Preliminaries Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs). In § 5 , we introduce AutoAnchor to construct a manifold-proximal anchor in diffusion unlearning. 5 Design of AutoAnchor To fundamentally avoid the instability and bias problems in diffusion unlearning, the anchor generated by AutoAnchor must satisfy three key requirements. (R1) Non-Synonymous: It must not be a direct synonym of the target concept. For example, using “naked” as an anchor fails to unlearn the "nude" concept, because the two distributions largely overlap, leaving the target insufficiently suppressed. (R2) Semantic Alternative: It should be a valid semantic alternative related to the target concept. For example, using an irrelevant concept “Mickey Mouse” as an anchor to unlearn the “nude” concept offers no meaningful guidance and effectively behaves as unconditional noise. (R3) Manifold-Proximal: It should be manifold-proximal to the target concept to guide a stable unlearning direction, as demonstrated by our theoretical analysis in § 4 . In addition to the three requirements of the anchor above, the generation process itself must be automatic (to avoid manually introducing extra subjective bias and ensure scalability of unlearning) and efficient (acting as a lightweight preprocessing step). We adopt the same settings to ensure a fair comparison. Evaluation Metrics. Following standard evaluation protocols, we assess model performance using CLIP scores and the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID). A higher CLIP score indicates better text-image semantic alignment, while a lower FID indicates superior image quality. We evaluate the models based on two primary criteria: (1) Removal : The model should fail to generate the erased concept, resulting in a low CLIP score on target concept prompts. (2) Utility Preservation : The model must retain its general generative capabilities on non-target concepts, which requires maintaining high text-image alignment (a high CLIP score) alongside high image quality (a low FID score).
